blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Meta-analysis is the statistical combination of the results of several independent studies of the same question into one pooled estimate. It is usually the analysis stage of a systematic review, a review that finds, selects and appraises all eligible studies by a pre-specified, reproducible method.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Each study is reduced to two ingredients used throughout this book: an effect estimate (a mean difference, a log risk ratio, a log odds ratio) and its standard error (recall §6.7). A simple average of the estimates would treat a small, imprecise trial like a large, precise one and throw away what the SE says. Meta-analysis instead weights each study by the inverse of its variance, w = 1/SE², so precise studies count more. Ratio measures are pooled on the log scale, where their sampling distribution is closer to Normal (recall §10.6.4), and the result is exponentiated at the end.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Why inverse-variance weights? A weighted average ȳ = Σwᵢyᵢ/Σwᵢ of independent estimates has variance Σwᵢ²SEᵢ²/(Σwᵢ)². With wᵢ = 1/SEᵢ² this becomes Σwᵢ/(Σwᵢ)² = 1/Σwᵢ, and no other choice of weights gives a smaller variance. So

pooled estimate = Σwᵢyᵢ ÷ Σwᵢ, SE(pooled) = 1 ÷ √Σwᵢ.

Because Σwᵢ is larger than any single wᵢ, the pooled SE is smaller than every study’s own SE.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Ten trials each test whether an antenatal supplement reduces low birthweight. Each is small, with a wide CI. Pooled, they give one estimate whose CI is narrower than any single trial’s.

points.html: A meta-analysis is only as good as its studies. Pooling biased studies gives a more precise wrong answer: precision does not remove bias (recall §6.4). Bias in the design sense (systematic error in how studies select, measure or analyse people) is catalogued in §17.2; the risk of bias of each included study should be assessed before pooling.
The studies must answer a comparable question: similar populations, interventions, comparators and outcome definitions. Heterogeneity (§15.7.2) measures how far the results disagree beyond chance.
§15.7.1 draws the forest plot, §15.7.2 measures heterogeneity, §15.7.3 pools by fixed- and random-effects models, and §15.7.4 checks for missing studies and grades the evidence.

blocks.html: Forest Plot

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A forest plot shows each study’s effect estimate as a square, with a horizontal line for its 95% CI, and the pooled estimate as a diamond at the bottom whose width is the pooled CI. The square’s area is proportional to the study’s weight.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The plot shows, on one page, both the individual pieces of evidence and how they combine. A vertical line marks “no effect” (RR = 1, or a mean difference of 0). A CI that crosses it is compatible with no effect at the 5% level (recall §8.5). Ratio measures are drawn on a log axis: on it, an RR of 0.5 and an RR of 2 lie the same distance from 1, and each CI, computed as ln RR ± 1.96 SE, is symmetric about its square.

blocks.caption: Figure 15.9. Forest plot of six trials of a hypothetical intervention (risk ratios, log axis). Square area is proportional to the fixed-effect weight (right-hand column). The diamond is the fixed-effect pooled RR 0.83 (95% CI 0.77 to 0.90).

blocks.html: Trial 6 carries the most weight (31%) because it has the narrowest CI; trial 3 carries 6%. Three of the six CIs (trials 1, 3 and 6) exclude 1, three cross it, and the pooled CI, 0.77 to 0.90, is narrower than any trial’s.

points.html: Weight follows precision, not sample size as such: a large trial with few events can still have a wide CI.

The diamond is usually narrower than every study’s CI (Derivation, §15.7). Under a random-effects model (one that lets the true effect vary between studies, §15.7.3) with substantial heterogeneity it is wider than the fixed-effect diamond, and may be little narrower than the most precise study (§15.7.3).
Read the spread of the squares before the diamond: widely scattered, non-overlapping CIs warn that one pooled number may not describe the studies (§15.7.2).

blocks.html: Heterogeneity – I² and Q Statistic

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Heterogeneity is variation in the true effects of the studies beyond what sampling error alone would produce. Cochran’s Q tests H₀: all studies share one true effect. I² is the percentage of the total variation across studies that is due to heterogeneity rather than chance.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Even if every study estimated exactly the same true effect, their estimates would differ by sampling error (recall §6.4). Q asks whether they differ more than their SEs allow, for example because the studies had different populations, doses or outcome definitions. I² turns Q into a descriptive percentage that does not depend on the number of studies in the same way.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
With k studies, fixed-effect weights wᵢ and fixed-effect pooled estimate ȳ:

Q = Σ wᵢ(yᵢ − ȳ)².

Each term is a squared z-score, [(yᵢ − ȳ)/SEᵢ]². Under H₀, Q follows approximately χ² with df = k − 1 (one df is used by estimating ȳ; recall §5.7.2.4). A χ² variable has mean equal to its df, so under H₀ Q is expected to be about k − 1. The excess, Q − df, measures heterogeneity, and as a share of Q it gives

I² = (Q − df)/Q × 100%, set to 0 when Q < df (Higgins et al., 2003).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Three trials of a community intervention against childhood diarrhoea (data/meta_three_trials.csv):

Trial Intervention: events/n Control: events/n RR ln RR SE(ln RR)
A 38/400 56/400 0.68 −0.388 0.198
B 60/450 64/450 0.94 −0.065 0.167
C 15/150 27/150 0.56 −0.588 0.301

SE(ln RR) = √(1/a − 1/n₁ + 1/c − 1/n₀) (recall §10.6.4). Trial A: √(1/38 − 1/400 + 1/56 − 1/400) = √0.0392 = 0.198.

points.html: Q has low power when studies are few or small. A non-significant Q is not evidence of no heterogeneity. For this reason p < 0.10, rather than 0.05, is sometimes used (Higgins et al., 2003; Cochrane Handbook, ch. 10). With k = 3, p = 0.23 says little.

I² labels are tentative conventions. Higgins et al. (2003) “tentatively” called 25%, 50% and 75% low, moderate and high. The Cochrane Handbook gives overlapping bands: 0–40% might not be important, 30–60% moderate, 50–90% substantial, 75–100% considerable, and adds that importance depends on the size and direction of the effects and the strength of evidence for heterogeneity. Here I² = 32.8% lies in the overlap of the first two bands; its CI would be very wide with three trials.
I² is a proportion, not an amount. It grows as the studies get larger (smaller SEs), even if the spread of true effects is unchanged. τ (§15.7.3) measures the spread itself.

Judgement comes first. Whether the studies are similar enough in population, intervention and outcome to share one true effect is decided on clinical and methodological grounds before looking at I². I² can confirm or challenge that judgement; it should not make it by a cut-off (“I² over 50%, so random effects”).
Explore, do not just report. When heterogeneity is present, prespecified subgroup analyses (by baseline risk, dose, setting) can suggest why, and the pooled estimate is interpreted with caution.

blocks.html: Fixed vs Random Effects Models

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A fixed-effect model assumes that every study estimates one common true effect and that the studies differ only by sampling error. A random-effects model assumes that the true effects themselves vary across studies around a mean, with between-study variance τ², and estimates that mean. A prediction interval gives the range in which the true effect of a new, similar study is expected to lie.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The phrase “random effects” appeared in §15.2.3 for patients nested in clusters (recall: cluster-specific values treated as draws from a shared distribution). Here the “clusters” are studies. In a random-effects model each study’s estimate has two sources of variance: its own sampling variance SE² and the between-study variance τ². The weights become 1/(SE² + τ²). Because τ² is added to every study, the weights become more equal: small studies gain relative weight, large studies lose it, and the pooled CI widens.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
DerSimonian–Laird estimate of τ². Under heterogeneity, Q exceeds its null expectation df = k − 1. Setting the expected value of Q equal to its observed value and solving (DerSimonian & Laird, 1986) gives

τ² = max{0, (Q − df) ÷ [Σwᵢ − Σwᵢ²/Σwᵢ]}.

Random-effects pooling. wᵢ* = 1/(SEᵢ² + τ²); pooled μ̂ = Σwᵢyᵢ/Σwᵢ; SE(μ̂) = 1/√Σwᵢ*.

Prediction interval. A new study’s true effect varies around μ with variance τ², and μ itself is estimated with variance SE(μ̂)². Adding them: μ̂ ± t × √(τ² + SE(μ̂)²), where Higgins et al. (2009) use t with k − 2 df. A z-value (1.96) is also used (the metafor default).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Pooling the three diarrhoea trials of §15.7.2 both ways.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Fixed-effect weights. Variances: A 0.198² = 0.0392, B 0.0278, C 0.0904. Weights: 25.5, 35.9, 11.1; Σw = 72.5 (percentages 35.2, 49.5, 15.3).
  2. Fixed-effect pooled. Σwy = 25.5 × (−0.388) + 35.9 × (−0.065) + 11.1 × (−0.588) = −18.72; ȳ = −18.72/72.5 = −0.258. SE = 1/√72.5 = 0.117. 95% CI: −0.258 ± 1.96 × 0.117 = −0.488 to −0.028. Back-transformed: RR 0.77 (0.61 to 0.97).
  3. τ². Σw² = 25.5² + 35.9² + 11.1² = 2,064; Σw − Σw²/Σw = 72.5 − 28.5 = 44.0. τ² = (2.98 − 2)/44.0 = 0.0222 (τ = 0.149 on the ln RR scale).
  4. Random-effects weights. 1/(0.0392 + 0.0222) = 16.3; 1/(0.0278 + 0.0222) = 20.0; 1/(0.0904 + 0.0222) = 8.9; Σ = 45.2 (percentages 36.1, 44.2, 19.7). Trial C’s share rises from 15% to 20%.
  5. Random-effects pooled. μ̂ = −0.284; SE = 1/√45.2 = 0.149. 95% CI −0.576 to 0.008. RR 0.75 (0.56 to 1.01). The random-effects CI now crosses 1.
  6. Prediction interval. √(0.0222 + 0.149²) = 0.211. With z: −0.284 ± 1.96 × 0.211 → RR 0.50 to 1.14. With t on k − 2 = 1 df (t = 12.71): 0.05 to 10.9, useless, which is the honest message: three trials cannot say how much the effect varies between settings.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
library(metafor)
d  <- read.csv("data/meta_three_trials.csv")
es <- escalc("RR", ai = events_int, n1i = n_int,
                   ci = events_ctl, n2i = n_ctl,
             data = d, slab = study)
fe <- rma(yi, vi, data = es, method = "FE")
re <- rma(yi, vi, data = es, method = "DL")
re
predict(re, transf = exp)
forest(re, atransf = exp)          # forest plot on a log axis
Random-Effects Model (k = 3; tau^2 estimator: DL)
tau^2 (estimated amount of total heterogeneity): 0.0222 (SE = 0.0681)
tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):      0.1490
I^2 (total heterogeneity / total variability):   32.83%
...
Test for Heterogeneity:
Q(df = 2) = 2.9774, p-val = 0.2257
Model Results:
estimate      se     zval    pval    ci.lb   ci.ub    
 -0.2841  0.1488  -1.9092  0.0562  -0.5757  0.0076  . 
...
   pred  ci.lb  ci.ub  pi.lb  pi.ub 
 0.7527 0.5623 1.0076 0.4982 1.1372

escalc("RR") computes each trial’s ln RR (yi) and its variance (vi, the SE² of the table). τ² = 0.0222, I² = 32.83% and Q = 2.98 (p = 0.23) are steps 3 and §15.7.2. The model estimate −0.284 (SE 0.149) is step 5 on the log scale; predict(..., transf = exp) back-transforms it to RR 0.75 (0.56 to 1.01) and gives the z-based prediction interval 0.50 to 1.14 (step 6). rma(method = "FE"), printed the same way, gives step 2.

points.html: Fixed-effect weights follow precision; random-effects weights are more equal. Large studies dominate a fixed-effect analysis. When small studies differ systematically from large ones (§15.7.4), a random-effects analysis gives them more influence, which can be a disadvantage.

Only the random-effects model widens the CI. A fixed-effect model estimates one common effect and does not widen its CI for heterogeneity. A random-effects model estimates the mean of a distribution of true effects, and its CI (and more so its prediction interval) reflects the variation between studies.

The two models answer different questions. Fixed effect: “what is the common effect in these studies?” Random effects: “what is the average effect across settings like these?” The prediction interval answers “what might happen in the next setting?” Riley et al. (2011) recommend reporting it; it “can be calculated when the meta-analysis contains at least three studies, although the interval may be very wide with so few studies”, as step 6 shows.

Choose on substantive grounds, before seeing the result. Picking whichever model gives the more favourable answer is results-driven analysis, like choosing a one-tailed test after the data (recall §8.6). When the choice is uncertain, report both as a sensitivity analysis and say whether the conclusion changes: here fixed effect 0.77 (0.61 to 0.97) and random effects 0.75 (0.56 to 1.01) differ in whether the CI excludes 1, so the conclusion is fragile.
τ² is itself poorly estimated with few studies (here SE 0.068 against an estimate of 0.022).

blocks.label: Checkpoint 15.11

questions.prompt: A meta-analysis of ten trials shows I² = 68%. A colleague says: “I² is over 50%, so we must use a random-effects model.” What reasoning does this shortcut, and what should come first?
questions.answer: The model should be chosen before the data are pooled, on clinical and methodological grounds: are the trials similar enough in population, intervention, comparator and outcome definition to share one true effect? If not, or if in doubt, a random-effects model (estimating the mean of a distribution of true effects) fits the question. I² can then confirm or challenge that judgement, but it is a descriptive proportion with conventional, overlapping bands (Higgins et al., 2003; Cochrane Handbook), not a switch. I² = 68% should also prompt a search for the sources of heterogeneity (prespecified subgroups) and a prediction interval.

questions.prompt: A forest plot’s pooled diamond is narrower than every study’s CI. Explain why, using inverse-variance weights. When might a random-effects diamond be barely narrower than the most precise study?
questions.answer: Each study gets weight wᵢ = 1/SEᵢ², and the pooled estimate Σwᵢyᵢ/Σwᵢ has SE = 1/√Σwᵢ. Because Σwᵢ exceeds every single wᵢ, the pooled SE is smaller than every study’s SE, and the pooled CI narrower. Under a random-effects model each weight becomes 1/(SEᵢ² + τ²). When τ² is large compared with the SEᵢ², every weight is limited by τ², the pooled SE is about √(τ²/k) or more, and the diamond can be little narrower than, or even wider than, the most precise study’s CI.

questions.prompt: Five studies give Q = 12.0. Compute I². Another five-study meta-analysis gives Q = 3.0: what is I², and why is it reported as that value?
questions.answer: df = k − 1 = 4. I² = (12.0 − 4)/12.0 = 8/12 = 66.7%. For Q = 3.0: (3.0 − 4)/3.0 = −33%, which is truncated to I² = 0%. Under H₀ (no heterogeneity), Q is expected to be about its df, and chance alone often makes it smaller. A negative excess means no evidence of heterogeneity, and a proportion of variance cannot be negative.

blocks.html: Publication Bias, Funnel Plots and PRISMA/GRADE

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Publication bias (more generally, non-reporting bias) arises when whether a study is published, or which results it reports, depends on its findings. Small-study effects are the tendency of smaller studies to show larger effects, for whatever reason. A funnel plot plots each study’s effect estimate against a measure of its precision (usually its SE, with the axis reversed). Egger’s test is a regression test for funnel-plot asymmetry. Trim-and-fill estimates how many studies may be missing and imputes them to give an adjusted pooled estimate.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Small trials have wide sampling scatter. If all were published, their results would spread evenly on both sides of the pooled effect, wider at the bottom of the plot (large SE) and narrower at the top: an inverted funnel. If small trials that happened to find no benefit stay in desk drawers, one lower corner of the funnel is empty, and the pooled estimate is pulled towards a larger benefit.

Asymmetry does not prove publication bias. Smaller studies may also be of poorer quality (which tends to exaggerate effects), may have been done in higher-risk populations where the true effect is larger (real heterogeneity), or the asymmetry may be chance.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html: Egger’s test. If there is no small-study effect, every study estimates the same θ, and its z-score yᵢ/SEᵢ = θ × (1/SEᵢ) + noise: a straight line through the origin when plotted against precision 1/SEᵢ. Egger et al. (1997) regress the “standard normal deviate” yᵢ/SEᵢ on 1/SEᵢ. An intercept away from 0 means that the least precise studies sit systematically on one side: asymmetry. (An equivalent form, used by R’s metafor package, regresses yᵢ on SEᵢ with weights 1/SEᵢ² and tests the slope on SE.)

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A simulation makes the mechanism visible. Forty trials of an intervention whose true RR is 0.85 are generated, with 25 to 800 children per arm. Every trial with a significant benefit is “published”, as is every trial with more than 400 per arm; each of the rest is published with probability 0.2. Seventeen trials are published.

blocks.caption: Figure 15.10. Funnel plots of 40 simulated trials (true RR 0.85). Left: all trials conducted, symmetric about the pooled RR 0.84. Right: the 17 “published” trials. Small trials to the right of the pooled line (no benefit) are missing, and the random-effects pooled RR moves to 0.80. Dashed lines: pooled ln RR ± 1.96 SE.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. All 40 trials: random-effects RR 0.84, close to the true 0.85.
  2. The 17 published trials: RR 0.80 (95% CI 0.72 to 0.89). The benefit is overstated: a 20% risk reduction instead of 16%.
  3. Egger’s test on the published trials: p = 0.004, strong evidence of asymmetry.
  4. Trim-and-fill imputes 3 missing trials on the right, and the adjusted RR is 0.82 (0.72 to 0.94), partly corrected.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
library(metafor)
# simulated: 40 trials, true RR 0.85
set.seed(33)
# children per arm
n   <- round(exp(runif(40, log(25), log(800))))
es  <- escalc("RR", ai = rbinom(40, n, 0.17), n1i = n,
                    ci = rbinom(40, n, 0.20), n2i = n)
es$pub <- es$yi/sqrt(es$vi) < -1.96 | n > 400 | runif(40) < 0.2
# the 17 "published" trials
pub <- rma(yi, vi, data = es[es$pub, ], method = "DL")
all40 <- rma(yi, vi, data = es, method = "DL")   # all 40 trials
round(exp(c(all = coef(all40), published = coef(pub))), 2)
regtest(pub, model = "lm")                     # Egger's test
trimfill(pub)
      all.intrcpt published.intrcpt 
             0.84              0.80 
Regression Test for Funnel Plot Asymmetry
Model:     weighted regression with multiplicative dispersion
Predictor: standard error
Test for Funnel Plot Asymmetry: t = -3.3788, df = 15, p = 0.0041
...
Estimated number of missing studies on the right side: 3 (SE = 2.7999)
Random-Effects Model (k = 20; tau^2 estimator: DL)
...
Model Results:
estimate      se     zval    pval    ci.lb    ci.ub     
 -0.1934  0.0681  -2.8385  0.0045  -0.3270  -0.0599  **

The first line compares steps 1 and 2. regtest(model = "lm") is Egger’s test in its weighted-regression form (step 3): the SE of each trial predicts its effect, t = −3.38 on 15 df. trimfill adds 3 imputed trials (k = 20) and re-pools: exp(−0.193) = 0.82, CI exp(−0.327) to exp(−0.060) = 0.72 to 0.94 (step 4). The “SE = 2.80” beside the 3 missing trials shows how uncertain that number is. funnel(pub) draws the plot.

points.html: At least 10 studies. Tests for funnel-plot asymmetry “should be used only when there are at least 10 studies”, because their power is low with fewer (Cochrane Handbook, ch. 13). The three-trial example of §15.7.3 cannot be assessed this way. Egger et al. (1997) themselves warned that results from “a limited number of small trials” need “considerable caution”.

Asymmetry is not diagnosis. The Cochrane Handbook states that funnel-plot asymmetry “should not be considered to be diagnostic for the presence of non-reporting bias”; heterogeneity, poor quality of small studies and chance produce it too.

Trim-and-fill is a sensitivity analysis, not a correction. Its adjusted estimate assumes the asymmetry is due to publication bias (Duval & Tweedie, 2000). With large heterogeneity and no publication bias it can distort the estimate, and its performance varies widely, so Peters et al. (2007) recommend it “as a form of sensitivity analysis as intended by the authors of the method”. Report it beside, not instead of, the main estimate.
Prevention beats detection. Searching trial registries (CTRI in India, ClinicalTrials.gov), theses and grey literature, and contacting authors, finds unpublished studies directly.
PRISMA 2020 is the reporting guideline for systematic reviews: a 27-item checklist and a flow diagram showing records identified, screened, excluded (with reasons) and included (Page et al., 2021).

GRADE rates the certainty of a body of evidence for each outcome as high, moderate, low or very low. Randomised trials start as high and observational studies as low; certainty is lowered for risk of bias (study limitations), inconsistency (heterogeneity, §15.7.2), indirectness, imprecision (a wide CI, as in §15.7.3) and publication bias (Guyatt et al., 2008).

blocks.label: Checkpoint 15.12

questions.prompt: A meta-analysis of six trials reports “Egger’s test p = 0.31, so there is no publication bias.” Give two reasons this conclusion is unsafe.
questions.answer: 1. With six studies the test has very low power; the Cochrane Handbook advises such tests only when there are at least 10 studies. A non-significant result is not evidence of absence. (ii) The test detects funnel-plot asymmetry, not publication bias as such: bias can exist without asymmetry (for example, if large as well as small null studies are unpublished), and asymmetry can arise without bias (heterogeneity, poorer quality of small studies, chance). A search of trial registries and grey literature says more about missing studies than the test does.

questions.prompt: In a meta-analysis of 12 trials, the four smallest (SE of ln RR 0.50 each) report RRs of 0.40 to 0.50, and the eight largest (SE 0.10 each) cluster around 0.90. Compute the share of the total fixed-effect weight carried by the four small trials. Would a random-effects analysis increase or decrease their influence, and why does that matter here?
questions.answer: Weights: small trials 1/0.50² = 4 each, 16 in total; large trials 1/0.10² = 100 each, 800 in total. Share = 16/816 = 2.0%. The fixed-effect estimate is essentially that of the large trials (about 0.90). The small and large trials clearly disagree, so τ² will be positive. A random-effects model adds τ² to every variance, making the weights more equal and increasing the small trials’ influence, pulling the pooled RR towards 0.4–0.5. Here the disagreement follows study size (a small-study effect, possibly publication bias), so the random-effects estimate would be the more misleading one. Report both and discuss why the small trials differ.

questions.prompt: Trim-and-fill imputes four “missing” trials and moves the pooled RR from 0.70 to 0.82. A colleague writes “the true effect is RR 0.82”. How would you rewrite the sentence?
questions.answer: “The pooled RR was 0.70 (with its CI). The funnel plot was asymmetric; in a sensitivity analysis assuming the asymmetry reflects unpublished studies, trim-and-fill imputed four trials and gave an RR of 0.82 (with its CI). The effect may therefore be overestimated.” Trim-and-fill assumes that the asymmetry is caused by publication bias and that the imputed studies mirror the observed ones; its estimate is a sensitivity analysis (Peters et al., 2007), not the true effect.
